WMU260 Aerial Ungulate Survey (201 6) 
Background 
Wildlife management unit (WMU) 260, located in east-central Alberta has a significant amount of 
agricultural area and contains the Saddle Lake Reserve. It is approximately 2011 km2 in size. Key 
ungulate habitat can be found along the North Saskatchewan River, which traverses the unit from the 
northwest to southeast and in a patch of crown land in the northeast portion of the unit.  
 
The most recent surveys in the unit were completed using the block survey method. For the 1998 
survey, a population estimate was created for white-tailed deer, with an estimate of 2,165. Thirty-seven 
mule deer, one elk, and eleven moose were counted during that survey but numbers and distribution 
relative to block flown precluded population estimates.  
There is currently an archery season with general licence for antlered and antlerless white-tailed deer 
and mule deer (Sept 1 – Oct 31). General licences for white-tailed deer (antlered and antlerless) are also 
available during the general season. Antlered and antlerless moose are on special licence during both 
archery and general seasons.  
 
Mule deer are on special licence during the general season. Elk in this unit are managed as part of a 
superunit (252, 254, 258, 260) and are on general licence during archery season and special licence 
during general season. Hunter harvest data for special licences indicate three year average success of: 
antlered moose 52%, antlerless moose 59%, antlered mule deer 43%, antlerless mule deer 50% and for 
elk in the WMU252/254/258/260 superunit: antlered elk 44%, and antlerless elk 46%.    
The objectives of this survey were to assess the status of the deer and moose populations for WMU 260, 
and to determine a population estimate for mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose based on density 
estimates, and a population split for sex and age classes for all three species.  
Survey Method 
The transect survey was conducted flying north-south lines at 1.6 km (1 mile) intervals for 25% coverage 
using 400m wide survey strips during January 18-22, 2016. Observers counted animals for the full length 
of each line transect. Animals were counted by species and identified by age and sex when possible. In 
addition to this, male u ngulates had their antlers classified as small (spike or 2 points on one or both 
antlers), medium (3 or more points with antlers inside their ears), or large (4 or more points and antlers 
outside of the ears) when possible.  
 
Due to the variation in transect lengths, population estimates were determined by Jolly’s (1969) method 
for sampling unequal sized units without replacement (Krebs 2014). Because of the timing of this survey 
some antler drop is expected to have happened, resulting in a male -skewed unclassified portion of the 
population, in particular for mule and white-tailed deer.

Results 
The survey covered 510 km2 , which encompassed 25% of the wildlife management unit. Moose, mule 
deer, and white-tailed deer were counted during the survey but no elk were observed.  Coyotes and 
foxes were also observed during the survey.   
 
There were 553 white-tailed deer observed within 188 groups. Of the 553 white-tailed deer observed 13 
(2%) were bucks, 232 (42%) were does, 230 (42%) were fawns and 78 (14 %) were not classified . Of the 
13 bucks identified, 6 (46%) were classified as small, 2 (15%) medium, and 5 (38%) large.  The buck: doe 
ratio was 0.06 and the fawn: doe ratio was 0.99 (Table 1). The average white-tailed deer density in WMU 
260 was estimated at 1.08 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 2181 + 313. This 
corresponds to a white-tailed deer population split estimate of 51 bucks, 915 does, 907 fawns, and 308 
unknown. 
 
There were 173 mule deer observed within 33 groups. Of the 173 mule deer counted,  24 (14%) were 
bucks, 23 (13 %) were does, 41 (24%) were fawns and 85 (49%) were not classified. Of the 24 bucks 
observed, 9 (38%) were classified as small, 6  (25%) medium, and 9 (38%) large. The buck: doe ratio was 
1.04 and the fawn: doe  ratio was 1.78 (Table 2).  The average mule deer  density in WMU 254 was 
estimated at 0.34 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate  of 682 + 222 (Table 2). This 
corresponds to  a mule deer  population split estimate of 94 bucks, 91 does, 162 fawns, and 335 
unknown. 
 
There were 84 moose observed within 44 groups. Of the 84 moose identified 6 (7%) were bulls, 41 (49%) 
were cows, and 37 (44%) were calves. The bull: cow ratio was 0.15 and the calf: cow ratio was 0.90 
(Table 3).  The average moose density in WMU 254 was estimated at 0.16 individuals/km2. This resulted 
in an abundance estimate of 331 + 81 (Table 3). This corresponds to moose population split estimate of 
24 bulls, 162 cows, and 146 calves.
